# Discussion

This study derived functional player roles for nine EuroLeague seasons from open data and found that five roles — ball handler, wing, stretch forward, interior big and rim protector — were reproducible under player-level resampling and across periods, whereas finer partitions were not. The roles overlapped with registered positions at the guard and centre extremes but not in between. Role labels added a small amount of information about lineup performance beyond regularised player ratings, but this came from the roles of the individual players, not from synergies between roles.

The five roles correspond to those most often reported in the literature. The systematic review by Coma Ribes et al. lists floor generals, shooters, versatile players and paint protectors among its recurrent roles and attributes much of the variation between studies to methodological heterogeneity [@ribes2026identifying]. The number of roles reported elsewhere ranges from three in the women's EuroLeague [@pendolareinecke2025exploring] to nine with box-score data [@ibanez2025redefining; @penner2025player; @kalman2020lineup], and low reproducibility of archetypes has been reported before [@penner2025player]. Our results suggest that, with box-score, shot-location and assist-network information, partitions finer than five roles are not reproducible, and that assist relationships are what make a five-role partition stable. The instability of a seven-cluster solution on the same data shows that internal validity indices alone do not guarantee a reproducible partition, which supports the review's call for a common standard [@ribes2026identifying]. Finer distinctions are likely to require play-type or tracking information.

The claim that modern basketball is "positionless" was only partly supported. Ball handlers and rim protectors remained tied to the guard and centre positions, whereas wings, stretch forwards and interior bigs each combined two registered positions. This agrees with the convergence of power forwards and centres documented in the EuroLeague [@konca2026from] and with compositional descriptions of position in the NBA [@south2024basketball], and suggests that positionless play is a property of the middle of the positional spectrum rather than of the game as a whole.

The lineup analysis separated two ideas that are often conflated: that some roles are worth more than RAPM credits them with, and that some role combinations are worth more than the sum of their parts. Only the first was supported. Role counts improved out-of-time predictions beyond RAPM, whereas pairwise role terms added nothing, although the power analysis shows that even small synergies for common pairings would have been detected. A plausible explanation for the main effects is that ridge regression shrinks every player toward the same value, so systematic differences between roles — rim protectors and ball handlers had the highest RAPM — are only partly recovered and are picked up by the role labels. This points to role-informed priors as a way to improve plus-minus estimates, in line with recent work that uses player-level information as priors for lineup ratings [@petridis2026lineup]. Earlier links between roles and success were established without adjusting for the quality of the players involved: lineup net rating was modelled from soft cluster memberships alone and was not validated out of sample [@kalman2020lineup], semi-final qualification was regressed on team role counts without player efficiency or playing time [@chen2023modeling], and role proportions were derived from players selected on high plus-minus [@penner2025player]. Our sensitivity analysis shows how apparent role-combination effects can also arise from the way lineups are observed: when very short lineups were included, the selected "significant" combinations were almost all negative, because lineups that concede runs are substituted quickly, and with a minimum duration their number fell to the level expected by chance. Together with evidence that lineup quality can be predicted from individual player quality [@martonosi2023predicting], the results suggest that a good lineup is, to a first approximation, a lineup of good players whose roles carry some information about their value.

## Limitations

Segment-level net rating is very noisy, and all models explained little variance in absolute terms; the composition gain was statistically detectable but small, and its exact size depended on how roles were defined. Because the permutation test carries the same noise as the observed data, the comparison with randomly assigned roles is nevertheless fair, and the power analysis shows that the absence of synergy is not simply a lack of sensitivity for common role pairings; for rarer pairings, smaller effects cannot be excluded. Only pairwise role interactions were tested, because higher-order combinations cannot be estimated in samples of this size; play-type data would allow such tests. Defensive behaviour was represented only indirectly by steals, blocks, rebounds and fouls, and the variable set was refined during exploration; however, the partition was almost unchanged when height was added, which indicates that the roles are not an artefact of a single variable group. The wing role was the least stable and should be used descriptively; the lineup results were the same with the four-role solution, in which wings merge with neighbouring roles. Silhouette values were low, so roles are best interpreted as regions of a continuum; posterior probabilities are provided for analyses that require soft membership. Finally, the findings are specific to the EuroLeague, but because data and code are open, the analysis can be repeated directly in other leagues.

## Conclusions

Five functional roles describe EuroLeague players reproducibly from open data and remain tied to registered positions only at the guard and centre extremes. Role labels carry a little information about lineup performance beyond regularised player ratings, but there was no evidence that particular role combinations perform better than the sum of their players. Coaches and analysts can therefore use these roles to describe and scout players and to inform player ratings, while lineup decisions should start from the individual quality of the players available.
